stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her general practice in suburban Adelaide for a 6-week postnatal check. Her first baby was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 40 weeks and is exclusively breastfed and growing well. The practice nurse has administered the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) in the waiting room and the total score is 15. On item 10 (self-harm) she scored 0.

She tells you the last three weeks have felt "grey", she cries most days, sleep is broken beyond what the baby demands, and she finds no pleasure in things that previously interested her. She denies suicidal or infanticidal ideas, has no psychotic features, and eats reasonably. Her partner is supportive and she has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. Basic postnatal examination and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.History: 6 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, no bipolar history, no psychosis, no suicidal/infanticidal ideas
data_table.Examination: Postnatal examination within normal limits; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that this represents normal baby blues resolving spontaneously and arrange telephone review with the practice nurse in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Baby blues resolve by day 10-14 and do not produce an EPDS of 15; her symptoms have persisted for 3 weeks at 6 weeks postpartum. Would never be correct (Source: Beyond Blue COPE perinatal guideline).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Repeat the EPDS in 2 weeks before making any diagnostic decision or committing to psychological or pharmacological management
options.rationale: An EPDS of at least 13 with 3 weeks of pervasive symptoms already meets the threshold for further clinical assessment and treatment planning today; delaying loses treatment weeks. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Undertake structured clinical assessment for perinatal depression and commence psychological therapy, with sertraline added if moderate or worse
options.rationale: The COPE Australian perinatal guideline treats an EPDS score of at least 13 as a positive screen requiring a structured clinical assessment (not a diagnosis in itself). With 3 weeks of pervasive anhedonia and low mood at 6 weeks postpartum, moderate perinatal depression is likely; stepped care starts with psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) with sertraline added for moderate or severe presentations because sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same-day psychiatric review and consideration of inpatient admission to a mother-baby unit
options.rationale: Acute team referral is reserved for suicidal or infanticidal ideation, psychotic features, or severe functional collapse; she has none of these. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg orally daily as first-line pharmacotherapy and continue breastfeeding without further specialist monitoring
options.rationale: Paroxetine is not preferred in breastfeeding when a naive start is being made; sertraline is favoured because of its very low relative infant dose. Would never be correct as first-line in a breastfeeding woman (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet
Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: An EPDS score of at least 13 is a positive screen for perinatal depression per the COPE Australian guideline and triggers a structured clinical assessment and stepped-care management, not simple reassurance or repeat screening.
key_points: EPDS at least 13 = positive screen; EPDS 10-12 = borderline (repeat in 2-4 weeks)
Baby blues peak day 3-5 and resolve by day 10-14
Item 10 = self-harm; any positive score triggers immediate safety assessment
Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (lowest relative infant dose)
Screen for bipolar and psychosis before starting any antidepressant
explanation.pearls: The EPDS screens for anxiety as well as depression; a moderate score with prominent anxious items should still be taken as a positive screen. In context: perinatal depression at 6 weeks postpartum with a screen-positive EPDS deserves the same rigour as any new episode of major depression, calibrated to the safety of the mother-infant dyad (Source: COPE).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet
Australian Medicines Handbook

stem:
A 28-year-old primipara is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 9 days postpartum by her mother. Her pregnancy and vaginal birth were uncomplicated. Over the last 48 hours she has slept less than 3 hours per night, become progressively agitated, and now insists that her baby's cry contains coded messages from her deceased grandmother telling her the baby must be "purified by water". She is fluctuating between elated and tearful within minutes.

She has a personal history of bipolar I disorder (last episode 4 years ago on lithium, ceased 8 months preconception with psychiatric agreement) and a maternal history of postpartum psychosis. On examination she is oriented but distractible with pressured speech; the baby is with her partner and appears well and feeding. Vital signs are within normal limits. Routine bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, calcium, TSH, glucose and CRP are within normal limits and urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Timeline: Day 9 postpartum; 48 h agitation, insomnia, delusions, mood lability
data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, last episode 4 years ago; mother had postpartum psychosis
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, corrected Ca, TSH, glucose, CRP within normal limits; UDS negative
data_table.Infant: With partner, feeding, no injuries reported

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly, provide a written safety plan, and arrange acute community mental health team review the following morning
options.rationale: Community follow-up cannot manage the acute infanticide and suicide risk of postpartum psychosis; delirium has been excluded and admission is required. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP perinatal position statement).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Admit as a psychiatric emergency (Mother-Baby Unit preferred where available), commence olanzapine, and reintroduce lithium after baseline bloods
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with substantial suicide and infanticide risk. RANZCP and COPE recommend admission to a specialist Mother-Baby Unit where available (or the nearest inpatient bed with arrangements to maintain the mother-infant relationship if no MBU) with an antipsychotic (olanzapine is commonly used) and reintroduction of a mood stabiliser such as lithium; ECT is considered for treatment resistance or life-threatening severity (Source: RANZCP; COPE; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture and MRI brain to exclude autoimmune or viral encephalitis before initiating any psychiatric admission or antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Organic screen is normal and the clinical picture (personal and family bipolar history, day 9 postpartum, characteristic mood-congruent psychosis) is classical for postpartum psychosis; further imaging is not needed before admission. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily, refer to community psychology for postnatal depression, and arrange partner-supervised follow-up in three days
options.rationale: Sertraline monotherapy can precipitate mania in bipolar patients and does not treat acute psychosis; the presentation is not depression. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Advise the partner and grandmother to supervise her at home for 24 hours, remove access to means, and represent immediately if symptoms worsen at all
options.rationale: Home supervision is inappropriate for postpartum psychosis regardless of a supportive partner. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis in a woman with bipolar I and a positive family history is a psychiatric emergency requiring urgent inpatient admission (ideally a Mother-Baby Unit) with antipsychotic and mood stabiliser therapy.
key_points: Peak onset days 3-14 postpartum, often abrupt
Personal or family history of bipolar or postpartum psychosis raises risk to about 1 in 2 in some cohorts
Suicide and infanticide risk is high and both dyad members need safeguarding
First-line: antipsychotic (often olanzapine) plus mood stabiliser (lithium if not breastfeeding a preterm or unwell infant; olanzapine or quetiapine if breastfeeding is prioritised)
ECT is highly effective and safe for severe or treatment-resistant cases
explanation.pearls: Always ask about family history of postpartum psychosis in any pregnant or newly postpartum woman with a mood disorder; it is one of the strongest predictors of recurrence. In context: rapid inpatient stabilisation preserves the mother-infant relationship better than delayed community care because untreated psychosis erodes early attachment and safety (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

subtopic_detail: Bipolar in pregnancy - lithium in the first trimester
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder that has been stable for 5 years on lithium modified-release 900 mg orally nightly (steady-state serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L) attends her GP at 6 weeks gestation after a positive home pregnancy test. Her last three episodes off lithium were severe manias, one requiring involuntary admission; two prior trials of valproate and lamotrigine each failed to prevent relapse within 4 months. She is otherwise well, plans to continue the pregnancy, and asks what to do about her medication.

She tells you she has read that lithium causes heart defects and wants to stop today. Renal function, thyroid function, and corrected calcium are within normal limits. Foetal ultrasound and dating are booked.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, stable 5 y on lithium; two prior alternative mood stabilisers ineffective
data_table.Current medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte, steady-state level 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: UEC, TSH, corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her lithium in the first trimester?

options.text: Continue lithium, arrange foetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-22 weeks, monitor serum lithium every 4 weeks with dose adjustment as pregnancy progresses
options.rationale: The absolute first-trimester risk of Ebstein anomaly with lithium is small (around 1 in 1000-2000, roughly 10-20 times baseline of 1 in 20 000). Her relapse risk without a mood stabiliser is very high with catastrophic consequences (previous severe mania, two failed alternatives). MotherToBaby Australia and RANZCP advise that continuing lithium is appropriate when alternatives have failed, with foetal cardiac imaging at 18-22 weeks and lithium monitoring every 4 weeks (more often in the third trimester because volume of distribution rises) (Source: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet; RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly today because of the risk of Ebstein anomaly, switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily, and rely on obstetric monitoring alone
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries about a 50% mania relapse risk within weeks; valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects) and contraindicated in pregnancy under the pregnancy prevention program. Would never be correct (Source: AMH; MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

options.text: Cross-taper lithium to lamotrigine 200 mg orally daily over 4 weeks with weekly review and no additional foetal cardiac imaging beyond the routine anatomy scan
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has already failed to prevent relapse in this patient; changing to a known-ineffective agent risks severe mania. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue lithium but empirically reduce the dose to 450 mg nocte to lower foetal exposure, without a maternal serum lithium level to guide the change
options.rationale: Empirically halving the dose neither meaningfully reduces first-trimester teratogenic risk (which is dose-related but the risk of a subtherapeutic level and relapse dominates) nor is guided by levels; dose changes should be driven by serum lithium. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

options.text: Stop lithium and rely on close psychiatric monitoring alone for the first trimester, restarting after 12 weeks only if she remains well and asymptomatic
options.rationale: Monitoring without prophylaxis in a patient with a high relapse rate and two failed alternatives exposes both mother and foetus to the far greater harm of untreated severe mania. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP; MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

explanation.summary: For a woman with severe bipolar I on lithium who has failed alternatives, the risk of untreated mania in pregnancy exceeds the small absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly; lithium is continued with foetal cardiac imaging at 18-22 weeks and serial level monitoring.
key_points: First-trimester lithium risk of Ebstein anomaly is about 1 in 1000-2000 (baseline 1 in 20 000)
Foetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-22 weeks is recommended for lithium-exposed pregnancies
Serum lithium falls in the second and third trimesters as volume of distribution rises; monitor 4-weekly then 2-weekly late pregnancy
Withhold or reduce lithium 24-48 h before planned delivery to avoid neonatal toxicity, restart postpartum
Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy (neural tube defects, later neurodevelopment)
explanation.pearls: The Ebstein statistic is a good example of relative-risk optics that ignore base rates; the absolute risk is small and the counter-risk of untreated severe mania is large. In context: shared decision-making about pregnancy and lithium requires framing risk in absolute terms and against the alternative of untreated illness (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Australian Medicines Handbook

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 3 weeks postpartum after a healthy term birth. She restarted lithium modified-release 900 mg nocte on day 2 postpartum on your advice and is currently well, with a maternal serum lithium of 0.7 mmol/L. Her infant is breastfeeding well, growing along the 50th percentile, and appears alert and hydrated.

Her partner has read online that lithium is "absolutely contraindicated" in breastfeeding and is anxious. She would strongly prefer to continue breastfeeding. The infant has no dysmorphism, no jitteriness, and no poor feeding; a paediatric review the previous day was unremarkable.

data_table.Maternal medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte; maternal serum Li 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Infant: Term, 3 weeks old, feeding well, growing along 50th percentile, no jitteriness or lethargy
data_table.Family concern: Partner concerned about breastfeeding on lithium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise she must stop breastfeeding immediately and switch to formula because lithium is absolutely contraindicated in lactation regardless of maternal preference
options.rationale: Lithium in breastfeeding is not absolutely contraindicated; it is a shared decision requiring monitoring, and abrupt cessation has psychological costs. Would never be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

options.text: Continue breastfeeding but empirically reduce her maternal lithium dose to 450 mg nocte to reduce infant exposure and repeat maternal levels in a fortnight
options.rationale: Empirical maternal dose reduction risks maternal relapse and does not reliably lower infant serum lithium; the standard is monitor not empirically reduce. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

options.text: Cross-taper her from lithium to olanzapine 15 mg nocte over 4 weeks so she can breastfeed safely, and cease all lithium once olanzapine is established
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not the preferred mood stabiliser for lithium-responsive bipolar I with a history of severe mania; switching a well patient introduces relapse risk without necessity. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue breastfeeding with informed consent, monitor infant serum lithium, UEC, and TSH at 2-4 weeks, and educate parents on signs of infant toxicity
options.rationale: Contemporary Australian sources (MotherToBaby Australia, RANZCP) accept breastfeeding on lithium with informed consent and paediatric involvement, provided the infant is term, healthy, and can be monitored. Infant serum lithium is usually 10-50% of maternal, and periodic infant lithium, renal, and thyroid function testing plus parental education on jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, and dehydration is the standard approach (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Recommend she express and discard breast milk for 4 hours after each lithium dose and then feed the infant to reduce peak lithium exposure through milk
options.rationale: Pump-and-dump timing does not appreciably reduce infant lithium exposure because lithium has a long half-life and is not confined to a peak; this is not a recognised strategy. Would never be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet

explanation.summary: Lithium in breastfeeding is acceptable in a well, term infant with monitoring; the older "absolutely contraindicated" teaching has been superseded by Australian and international perinatal guidance.
key_points: Infant serum lithium typically 10-50% of maternal
Monitor infant serum lithium, UEC, TSH at 2-4 weeks and then periodically
Educate parents on infant toxicity: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, dehydration
Highest-risk periods: hot weather, gastroenteritis, prolonged interfeed intervals
Weigh benefits of breastfeeding against benefits of maternal mood stability
explanation.pearls: Shared decision-making trumps blanket rules in perinatal psychopharmacology; the older lithium-in-breastfeeding taboo caused avoidable relapse. In context: preserving both maternal stability and breastfeeding is achievable in most well term dyads with appropriate monitoring (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Australian Medicines Handbook

stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 7 weeks gestation attends her GP with an escalating major depressive episode. This is a planned first pregnancy. She has a 4-year history of recurrent moderate to severe depression previously stabilised on paroxetine 20 mg orally daily, which she stopped 3 months before conception on her own initiative. She now reports 3 weeks of low mood, early morning waking, poor appetite, and thoughts that life is "not worth it" without a specific plan. She is not psychotic and has no bipolar history. Basic bloods and thyroid function are within normal limits.

She is willing to restart medication but has read that antidepressants "cause heart defects" in the first trimester and asks what is safest.

data_table.History: Recurrent MDD, 4 y; stopped paroxetine 3 months preconception
data_table.Current episode: 3 weeks moderate-severe depression, passive suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg orally daily because she previously responded to it, and refer for structured psychological therapy in parallel over 6 weeks
options.rationale: Paroxetine is best avoided if a naive start can be made in the first trimester because of a small increase in relative risk of cardiac malformations reported in several cohorts; sertraline is a safer restart in a woman not currently on paroxetine. Would rarely be correct at 7 weeks with no current exposure (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and refer for structured psychological therapy such as CBT or interpersonal therapy
options.rationale: Sertraline is the SSRI of choice when starting or restarting antidepressant therapy in the first trimester because the reproductive safety data are the most reassuring and it also has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk, providing continuity for postpartum feeding. Combined with structured psychological therapy this represents best-practice moderate-severe perinatal depression care (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Withhold pharmacotherapy for the first trimester and reassess mood, appetite, and suicidal ideation at 13 weeks with a repeat EPDS at that visit
options.rationale: Untreated moderate-severe depression in pregnancy carries meaningful risks (poor engagement with antenatal care, low birth weight, preterm birth, postpartum depression) and passive suicidal ideation is present. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg extended release orally daily as first-line perinatal antidepressant therapy with a plan to titrate up in 2 weeks if needed
options.rationale: SNRIs are second-line for perinatal depression; there is more experience with SSRIs and sertraline in particular. Would rarely be correct as first-line (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy as the safest treatment in pregnancy given her passive suicidal ideation and prior antidepressant responsiveness
options.rationale: ECT is safe in pregnancy but reserved for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression and severe suicidality with imminent risk; it is not first-line for moderate-severe depression that has not had a medication trial. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI when initiating or restarting antidepressant treatment in early pregnancy because reproductive safety data are most reassuring and continuity into breastfeeding is straightforward.
key_points: Sertraline: first-line SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding (low relative infant dose)
Paroxetine: avoid naive start in first trimester (small excess risk of cardiac malformations); may continue if already stable and switching risks relapse
Fluoxetine: long half-life, more accumulation in neonate
Neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress) can follow third-trimester SSRI exposure, usually self-limited
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: absolute risk small (about 3 per 1000 exposed vs 1-2 per 1000 unexposed)
explanation.pearls: The perinatal safety story of SSRIs has been overstated in lay media; framing risks in absolute terms and against the risks of untreated depression is central to informed consent. In context: sertraline is a reasonable default in most perinatal MDD presentations because it also carries safely into breastfeeding (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: ECT in pregnancy - severe depression with suicidality
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 24 weeks gestation is admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a tertiary maternal mental health unit with severe depression. She has psychomotor retardation, has stopped eating and drinking for the past 3 days requiring intravenous fluids, believes her foetus "is already dead" despite normal cardiotocograph tracings, and has begun to endorse a specific plan of self-strangulation. Adequate trials of sertraline (200 mg) and mirtazapine (45 mg) for 6 and 8 weeks respectively during this pregnancy have failed. Obstetric assessment shows a well foetus of appropriate size for gestational age. Bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs and TSH are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: Severe MDD with psychotic features, active suicidal plan, food refusal 3 days
data_table.Prior treatment: Sertraline 200 mg 6 wks; mirtazapine 45 mg 8 wks - both ineffective
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly to her current sertraline and mirtazapine, continue involuntary care, and reassess mood, suicidality, and oral intake in 4 weeks
options.rationale: A further 4-week medication trial is unsafe in the face of imminent suicidality, food refusal, and psychotic depression, and delays a definitive treatment. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Add lithium 750 mg nocte as augmentation, continue current antidepressants at maximum tolerated doses, and reassess her mood and suicidality over the next 2 weeks
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation would not act quickly enough for imminent suicidality and food refusal at 24 weeks; ECT is definitive. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Proceed with electroconvulsive therapy after joint obstetric-anaesthetic assessment, with left lateral tilt, airway protection, and pre- and post-treatment foetal monitoring
options.rationale: ECT is safe across all trimesters of pregnancy and is indicated for severe depression with psychotic features, active suicidality, treatment resistance, or food refusal endangering mother or foetus. Standard obstetric precautions apply: joint obstetric-anaesthetic assessment, left lateral tilt to prevent aortocaval compression, non-particulate antacid, avoidance of hyperventilation, and foetal heart rate monitoring pre- and post-ECT after viability (Source: RANZCP ECT clinical memorandum; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Commence intranasal esketamine 84 mg twice weekly as a rapid-acting antidepressant, continue current antidepressants, and monitor blood pressure after each dose
options.rationale: Esketamine is not established in pregnancy and PBS access does not cover this indication; safer, better-evidenced options exist. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Defer any definitive treatment change until after delivery, maintain her current sertraline and mirtazapine regimen, and continue one-to-one nursing observation
options.rationale: Deferring treatment risks maternal death and foetal loss; severe untreated depression in pregnancy is itself high-risk. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: ECT is safe and effective across pregnancy for severe treatment-resistant depression, psychotic depression, active suicidality, and food refusal, provided obstetric-anaesthetic precautions are observed.
key_points: ECT indications in pregnancy: severe suicidality, psychotic depression, catatonia, food refusal, treatment resistance, severe mania endangering pregnancy
Precautions: joint obstetric and anaesthetic assessment, left lateral tilt after 20 weeks, non-particulate antacid, avoid hyperventilation, foetal monitoring after viability
Response typically seen after 4-6 treatments; maintenance considered if history of relapse
Common side effects: retrograde amnesia (mostly reversible), transient headache, myalgia
explanation.pearls: ECT is often the safest treatment for the foetus in severe maternal illness because it avoids ongoing systemic drug exposure. In context: framing ECT as an active safety choice for the dyad, rather than a last resort, aligns with contemporary RANZCP practice (Source: RANZCP ECT memorandum).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australian Medicines Handbook

stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after 5 days of progressively pressured speech, minimal sleep, spending $12 000 on cryptocurrency, and grandiose delusions of being a "chosen prophet". He has a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder and admits to stopping his lithium 3 weeks ago. He is not on any other regular medication.

He is oriented but distractible with flight of ideas and paces the interview room. He denies suicidal or homicidal ideation and has no active plan of harm. He accepts oral medication. Vital signs: pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 C. Urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, TSH, and urine drug screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: 5 days manic symptoms; pressured speech, grandiose delusions, no suicidal or homicidal intent
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH, UDS within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Recommence lithium modified release 750 mg orally nocte as monotherapy, offer oral lorazepam 1 mg for sleep, and reassess mania severity clinically in 48 hours
options.rationale: Lithium monotherapy takes 1-2 weeks to reach therapeutic serum levels and clinical effect; acute mania needs faster tranquillising cover. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Give a single intramuscular droperidol 10 mg immediately for tranquillisation, physically restrain until sedated, and admit to a psychiatric intensive care unit
options.rationale: Parenteral rapid tranquillisation is reserved for patients unable to accept oral medication or with imminent behavioural risk; he is accepting oral medication and is not physically aggressive. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical care standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 1000 mg orally daily as monotherapy and discharge with community mental health follow-up in 3 days, with a partner-supervised safety plan
options.rationale: Discharge is inappropriate for acute mania under mental health apprehension with grandiose delusions and financial risk; valproate monotherapy also lacks the rapid tranquillising effect. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg or quetiapine 400 mg, reintroduce lithium once renal function is confirmed, and offer oral lorazepam 1-2 mg for agitation
options.rationale: Combination therapy of a mood stabiliser plus an SGA is more effective than either alone in acute mania; the SGA delivers rapid antimanic and tranquillising effect while lithium re-establishes prophylaxis. Oral lorazepam is used for adjunctive sedation when required. The RANZCP mood disorders CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic support this stepped approach (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Commence carbamazepine 400 mg orally twice daily with diazepam 10 mg orally three times daily and discharge with community psychiatric follow-up in one week
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is a third-line antimanic; diazepam accumulates and is not preferred for procedural sedation in acute mania (lorazepam is preferred for consistent kinetics). Would rarely be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Acute mania is managed with combination therapy: a rapidly-acting SGA plus a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate as appropriate), with adjunctive lorazepam for agitation, and admission where risk warrants.
key_points: First-line combination: SGA (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) plus mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate)
Lorazepam preferred over diazepam for adjunctive tranquillisation (no active metabolites, predictable half-life)
Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of reproductive potential unless the pregnancy prevention program is met
Screen for substance-induced mania (UDS) before attributing to bipolar
Admit under the Mental Health Act if insight is absent and there is risk to self, others, or reputation/finances
explanation.pearls: Reputation and financial catastrophe count as harm for the purposes of civil commitment assessment. In context: rapid combination therapy shortens time to remission and length of stay compared with monotherapy in acute mania (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS versus anticholinergic
stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department 6 hours after being started on tramadol 50 mg orally four times daily by his GP for acute back pain. His regular medications include venlafaxine 150 mg extended release daily (for depression, stable 2 years) and selegiline that was recently prescribed by a neurologist. He is agitated, sweating profusely, and complaining of jaw clenching.

On examination he is diaphoretic, has spontaneous bilateral lower limb clonus on ankle dorsiflexion (right greater than left), brisk reflexes throughout, hyperactive bowel sounds, and dilated but reactive pupils. Vital signs: pulse 128 bpm, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 C. He is oriented but restless.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, spontaneous lower limb clonus R>L, hyperreflexia, hyperactive bowel sounds, dilated reactive pupils, jaw clenching
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 150 mg XR, selegiline (recent), tramadol 50 mg qid (started 6 h ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive cooling, and admit to intensive care for supportive care
options.rationale: NMS produces lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, and a subacute onset (usually days) and is triggered by dopamine antagonists, which he is not on. The clonus, hyperreflexia, and rapid onset after serotonergic loading argue against NMS. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; RANZCP).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Anticholinergic toxicity; give IV physostigmine 1 mg with cardiac monitoring, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, and admit for continued observation overnight
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, and unreactive dilated pupils. He is diaphoretic with hyperactive bowel sounds and reactive pupils. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxicity from occult stimulant use; obtain a urine drug screen, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation, and manage supportively with cooling and fluids
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic toxicity does not classically produce clonus and hyperreflexia; his medications and the temporal relationship to tramadol point to serotonergic causation. Would rarely be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Panic attack with concurrent fever from a viral illness; give oral lorazepam 1 mg, provide paracetamol for the fever, reassess in an hour, and discharge if settled
options.rationale: Panic does not produce clonus, hyperreflexia, or temperature 39.2 C, and the medication sequence is diagnostic. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; cease all serotonergic agents, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, give benzodiazepines for agitation, consider cyproheptadine if severe
options.rationale: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are satisfied (spontaneous clonus in the presence of a serotonergic agent) and the classical triad of neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), and altered mental state is present after a serotonergic loading event. Australian toxicology practice is to cease serotonergic agents, provide supportive care with active cooling, generous IV fluids, and benzodiazepines for agitation and muscle activity; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist) is considered for persisting or severe symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AMH).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed by the Hunter criteria (serotonergic agent plus clonus, agitation with sweating, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with hyperthermia); management is cessation, cooling, fluids, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine for severe cases.
key_points: Onset within hours of a serotonergic dose change; neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia) is the key differentiator from NMS
MAOI + serotonergic (tramadol, SSRI, SNRI, meperidine) combinations carry the highest risk
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, days-scale onset, dopamine antagonist trigger
Anticholinergic toxidrome: hot dry red skin, unreactive dilated pupils, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention
Malignant hyperthermia: inhalational anaesthetic or succinylcholine trigger, family history
explanation.pearls: Tramadol is a common inadvertent trigger of serotonin syndrome because it combines opioid and serotonergic activity; check for MAOIs and SSRIs before prescribing. In context: distinguishing the hyperthermic toxidromes at the bedside prevents lethal misdiagnosis and dangerous treatments (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
Australian Medicines Handbook
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

stem: A 38-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought to a large metropolitan emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after threatening staff at a supported accommodation service. In the ED he is pacing, shouting at unseen figures, refusing to speak with staff, and has just struck a chair against the wall. Verbal de-escalation by a psychiatric nurse and a security officer for 10 minutes has been unsuccessful, and he refuses all oral medication. His weight is estimated at 90 kg, he has no known allergies, and there is no clear history of QT prolongation. Point-of-care ECG is not immediately available. He has not taken alcohol or benzodiazepines in the past 24 hours per accompanying support worker.

data_table.Presentation: Acute severe behavioural disturbance, active aggression, refusing oral medication
data_table.Relevant history: Schizophrenia, no known QT prolongation, no recent alcohol or benzodiazepine

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg, with strict avoidance of concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: The NSW Health clinical care standard for acute severe behavioural disturbance identifies IM olanzapine and IM droperidol as first-line options when parenteral rapid tranquillisation is required after failed de-escalation. IM olanzapine 10 mg is a defensible first choice; the specific safety flag is to avoid concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines because of respiratory depression risk. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is mandatory (Source: NSW Health ABD clinical care standard; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with intramuscular promethazine 50 mg, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and a baseline 12-lead ECG once feasible
options.rationale: The high-dose haloperidol/promethazine cocktail is not preferred in Australian practice; haloperidol has substantial QT and EPS risk and promethazine adds sedation and anticholinergic burden without clear benefit. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg as monotherapy, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway equipment ready at the bedside for the next 2 hours
options.rationale: IM midazolam monotherapy carries meaningful risk of respiratory depression, especially at 10 mg, and provides no antipsychotic effect for schizophrenic agitation. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Physical restraint alone until behaviour settles, with continuous nursing observation and reassessment for pharmacological therapy after 30 minutes if not settled
options.rationale: Physical restraint without pharmacological adjunct is unsafe, prolongs restraint time, and increases the risk of positional asphyxia and cardiac arrest; restraint is a last resort combined with, not instead of, pharmacological management. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Oral quetiapine 200 mg with continuous observation on a secure ward, and a further dose in 30 minutes if he remains agitated and continues to accept oral therapy
options.rationale: He refuses oral medication and behaviour is imminently unsafe; oral routes are inappropriate. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

explanation.summary: For acute severe behavioural disturbance in an adult after failed verbal de-escalation and refusal of oral medication, IM olanzapine or IM droperidol are first-line parenteral options per the NSW Health clinical care standard, with continuous monitoring and specific avoidance of concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines with IM olanzapine.
key_points: Verbal de-escalation is always the first step
First-line parenteral: IM olanzapine 10 mg OR IM droperidol 10 mg
Avoid concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines with IM olanzapine (respiratory depression)
Monitor SpO2, pulse, BP, RR, sedation, and airway continuously
Restraint is a last resort and always time-limited and documented
explanation.pearls: The IM olanzapine + IM benzodiazepine combination has caused deaths and is a specific pharmacovigilance warning. In context: rapid tranquillisation aims to keep the patient and staff safe while a definitive assessment can be conducted, not to sedate to unconsciousness (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).

subtopic: Suicide risk and Mental Health Act
stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought to a NSW emergency department by his sister after she found a suicide note on his kitchen table and a coiled rope in his shed. He has an 18-month history of severe major depressive disorder that has not responded to adequate trials of sertraline 200 mg then venlafaxine 300 mg. In interview he is guarded, describes his suicide plan in detail, states he still intends to act if discharged, and refuses admission because he believes he "deserves" to die.

He has no known psychiatric admission history and has capacity to understand the information you provide, but his depressive beliefs prevent him from choosing consistent with survival. He has no comorbid substance use and vital signs, basic bloods, and ECG are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: 18 months severe MDD, current plan and intent, refusal of voluntary admission
data_table.Prior treatment: Sertraline 200 mg, venlafaxine 300 mg - both ineffective
data_table.Assessment: Guarded, understands information, cognitive distortions dominate decision
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; ECG within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Discharge with an urgent GP appointment in 24 hours, a written safety plan, and a follow-up phone call from the community mental health team the following day
options.rationale: He has active intent, a specific plan and access to means, and refuses admission; community discharge is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP suicide prevention practice guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP suicide prevention practice guideline

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, arrange expedited psychiatric review for ECT consideration, and remove access to means
options.rationale: He meets the criteria for a mentally ill person under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 (mental illness with serious risk to himself) and refuses voluntary admission; involuntary admission is indicated. Expedited psychiatric review is required and ECT should be considered given severe treatment-resistant depression with active suicidality (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP suicide prevention guideline).
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Act 2007
RANZCP suicide prevention practice guideline
RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

options.text: Ask his sister to remove all sharps and the rope from home, provide constant one-to-one supervision at home for 72 hours, and represent immediately if any change
options.rationale: Family-supervised home safety is not a substitute for admission when a patient with severe depression has active intent and a plan; the burden on family and imperfect supervision fail. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP suicide prevention guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP suicide prevention practice guideline

options.text: Commence lithium augmentation 500 mg orally nocte, discharge with community mental health follow-up in 5 days, and a written safety plan with removal of means
options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe; lithium augmentation is a reasonable step but is not the immediate priority over admission. Would never be correct as the immediate step (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Because he has capacity, respect his refusal of admission, provide a Wellness Recovery Action Plan, and arrange community mental health follow-up in 48 hours
options.rationale: Legal capacity does not preclude involuntary admission for a mentally ill person under the NSW Mental Health Act when serious risk to self is present; this framing misapplies capacity law. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Act 2007

explanation.summary: Active suicidal intent with a specific plan, access to means, and refusal of voluntary admission in a patient with severe treatment-resistant MDD warrants involuntary admission under the applicable state Mental Health Act with removal of means and expedited access to definitive treatment including ECT.
key_points: Suicide risk assessment centres on ideation, intent, plan, access to means, and protective factors
Treatment-resistant depression = failure of two adequate antidepressant trials from different classes
ECT is highly effective and rapid in severe TRD with active suicidality
Involuntary admission requires mental illness, risk to self or others, and no less restrictive alternative
Capacity is not the sole determinant of admission under state Mental Health Acts
explanation.pearls: Removal of means (guns, rope, medications) is one of the highest-yield population-level suicide prevention interventions. In context: an active plan with access to means is functionally imminent risk irrespective of ambivalence during interview (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Act 2007
RANZCP suicide prevention practice guideline

subtopic_detail: ED assessment sequence after intoxicated self-poisoning
stem:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 90 minutes after ingesting 30 tablets of quetiapine 100 mg and drinking about 750 mL of wine following an argument with her partner. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, tearful, and asking to be discharged so she can go home. Vital signs: pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 C. Fingerstick glucose is 5.6 mmol/L, blood alcohol is 0.18 g/100 mL, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QTc 468 ms.

The on-call psychiatry registrar has been paged and asks whether she can be assessed for discharge planning now, as the department is very busy.

data_table.Ingestion: Quetiapine 30 x 100 mg tablets + ~750 mL wine, 90 min ago
data_table.Investigations: BSL 5.6 mmol/L, blood alcohol 0.18 g/100 mL, ECG sinus tachy QTc 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit to a monitored bed, provide cardiorespiratory monitoring and serial ECGs, and defer formal psychiatric risk assessment until she is medically cleared and clinically sober
options.rationale: The Royal Australian College of Emergency Medicine and NSW Health mental health emergency care standards mandate medical clearance before psychiatric assessment and require that structured risk assessment be undertaken when the patient is no longer intoxicated so that the assessment reflects sober cognition. Quetiapine overdose can cause delayed sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, and QT prolongation, warranting monitoring for at least 4-6 hours or until asymptomatic. Discharge against medical advice is not appropriate while intoxicated and drowsy (Source: ACEM mental health emergency care standard; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: ACEM mental health in the ED policy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
NSW Health Mental Health Emergency Care Interagency Agreement

options.text: Allow the psychiatry registrar to complete the mental state examination and structured risk assessment now to expedite disposition and free up the emergency department bed
options.rationale: Risk assessment while acutely intoxicated is unreliable and creates medico-legal exposure; her sobriety and medical stability must be established first. Would rarely be correct (Source: ACEM).
source_refs: ACEM mental health in the ED policy

options.text: Discharge with her partner because she is rousable and asking to leave, with a general practice appointment in 48 hours and a safety plan given to her partner
options.rationale: She is intoxicated, drowsy from a psychotropic overdose, with QTc 468 ms; discharge is unsafe and requires medical stabilisation and sober risk assessment. Would never be correct (Source: ACEM).
source_refs: ACEM mental health in the ED policy

options.text: Administer oral activated charcoal 50 g now to reduce quetiapine absorption, obtain airway protection with intubation if necessary, and repeat ECG in 2 hours
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is not indicated more than 1-2 hours post-ingestion for quetiapine and is unsafe in a drowsy patient without airway protection because of aspiration risk. Would never be correct at 90 minutes in a drowsy patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Apply an involuntary treatment order under the Mental Health Act to compel psychiatric admission today, without further medical work-up or observation of sobriety
options.rationale: Mental Health Act processes are not a substitute for medical clearance; a scheduled patient still requires medical stabilisation and a sober assessment before psychiatric disposition. Would rarely be correct as the immediate step (Source: ACEM; NSW MH Act).
source_refs: ACEM mental health in the ED policy
NSW Mental Health Act 2007

explanation.summary: After intoxicated deliberate self-poisoning the sequence is: medical stabilisation and monitoring, then structured psychiatric risk assessment once clinically sober (typically 4-6 hours) and medically cleared; risk assessment while intoxicated is unreliable.
key_points: Medical clearance first: airway, breathing, circulation, disability including glucose, ECG, and ongoing toxicity monitoring
Quetiapine overdose: sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation - monitor at least 4-6 h
Reassess risk and mental state when the patient is sober; sobriety changes intent in many cases
Involve family or supports and confirm collateral information at the time of assessment
Document capacity, risk factors, protective factors, and safety plan explicitly
explanation.pearls: Risk assessment scores do not predict individual behaviour reliably; clinical judgement plus collateral plus sober mental state remains the standard. In context: separating medical and psychiatric phases of ED care prevents both unsafe discharge and premature psychiatric commitment (Source: ACEM).

sources.label: ACEM mental health in the ED policy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
NSW Health Mental Health Emergency Care Interagency Agreement
NSW Mental Health Act 2007

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge and ECT if refractory
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her family after 4 days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and refusal of food and fluids. On examination she stares fixedly, does not respond to questions, holds her left arm in an awkward flexed position for several minutes when placed there by the examiner, and echoes fragments of the examiner's speech when she does speak. Her Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 14. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 C. Creatine kinase is 380 U/L (normal upper limit 200). Bloods, urine drug screen, TSH and CT brain are within normal limits.

The on-call psychiatry registrar administers 2 mg IV lorazepam under monitoring. Within 20 minutes she engages briefly, drinks a small volume of water, but returns to mutism after 90 minutes.

data_table.Presentation: 4 days progressive catatonic features (mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echolalia); BFCRS 14
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L; FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, UDS, CT brain within normal limits
data_table.Response to 2 mg IV lorazepam: Brief 20-min engagement then mutism returns at 90 min

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg to treat presumed underlying psychotic disorder, continue supportive care, and reassess her Bush-Francis score in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and NMS; they are avoided in acute catatonia until it has resolved and are not first-line. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Discharge her from the emergency department with community psychiatric follow-up in 48 hours, encouragement of oral intake at home, and family observation overnight
options.rationale: Persistent catatonia with food and fluid refusal is life-threatening; discharge is not safe. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

options.text: Commence scheduled lorazepam 2 mg orally or IM three times daily, ensure hydration and DVT prophylaxis, and refer for ECT if catatonia persists over 48-72 hours
options.rationale: A positive response to a lorazepam challenge (any partial improvement) confirms catatonia and justifies scheduled benzodiazepine therapy with escalating doses. Australian and international practice (RANZCP, Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic) recommends scheduled lorazepam 6-24 mg/day depending on response, with ECT if catatonia does not resolve within 48-72 hours or if malignant features develop. Supportive care includes hydration, DVT prophylaxis, and skin care (Source: RANZCP ECT memorandum; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome, admit to intensive care for cooling and monitoring, and stop all psychotropic agents
options.rationale: She has no dopamine antagonist exposure, no lead-pipe rigidity, and no hyperthermia; the CK is only mildly elevated from prolonged posturing. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Give a further single dose of lorazepam 4 mg IV as an escalated challenge, observe her for 24 hours in the emergency short-stay unit, and reassess before further action
options.rationale: A one-off larger dose without scheduled maintenance risks relapse of the catatonia; scheduled dosing (with monitoring for over-sedation) is the standard, not a single larger dose. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

explanation.summary: Catatonia responsive to a lorazepam challenge is managed with scheduled lorazepam titrated to effect (typically 6-24 mg/day) with ECT reserved for persistent, refractory, or malignant catatonia; antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia resolves.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale > 3 supports diagnosis; positive lorazepam challenge confirms
Waxy flexibility (catalepsy), mutism, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia, stupor - core features
Malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, altered mental state - proceed urgently to ECT
Avoid antipsychotics during acute catatonia (risk of NMS)
ECT is highly effective (about 80% response in retrospective series)
explanation.pearls: Catatonia is underdiagnosed in medical wards and is often mistaken for depression, delirium, or coma; a quick lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic. In context: catatonia in mood disorders responds particularly well to benzodiazepines and ECT (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

stem:
A 29-year-old primipara presents to her general practice on day 5 postpartum for a routine newborn check. She had a normal vaginal birth of a healthy term baby. She reports tearfulness that comes and goes over the past 3 days, mild irritability, difficulty sleeping when the baby is settled, and rapid mood swings but denies pervasive low mood or loss of interest. She has no suicidal or infanticidal thoughts, no psychotic features, and no history of psychiatric illness. She is breastfeeding and the baby is feeding and growing well. EPDS today is 9.

On examination she looks tired but engaged, cries briefly when describing the birth, then laughs when discussing the baby. Postnatal observations and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Symptoms: Transient tearfulness, mood lability, no anhedonia, no suicidal or psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order urgent thyroid antibodies, morning cortisol, and repeat TSH given that the most likely cause of this presentation is early postpartum thyroiditis and adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis typically presents from 3-6 months, TSH is within normal limits, and the clinical picture fits baby blues; further testing is not indicated (Source: RCPA thyroid function testing guide).
source_refs: RCPA thyroid function testing guide

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily now to prevent progression to postnatal depression, continue breastfeeding, and arrange community midwife review in 1 week
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not indicated for baby blues and would expose an infant to an unnecessary medication. Would never be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Refer urgently for perinatal psychiatry review today with a follow-up EPDS in 1 week and a plan to consider inpatient admission if any symptoms worsen or persist
options.rationale: There are no risk features (suicidal, infanticidal, psychotic, functional collapse) to justify urgent specialist review; primary care management is appropriate. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Recommend she stop breastfeeding to improve her sleep and mood, transition to formula feeding gradually over 1 week, and arrange lactation consultant support
options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is neither indicated nor supported by evidence for baby blues; sleep support strategies with the partner are preferred. Would never be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Reassure her that these symptoms are consistent with baby blues, provide psychoeducation and family support, and arrange EPDS repeat in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Baby blues affect around 50-80% of women, peak on days 3-5, and resolve by day 10-14; they do not require pharmacotherapy. EPDS of 9 (below 10) with transient symptoms fits the pattern. COPE advises psychoeducation, family support, and repeat EPDS in 2 weeks to catch evolving postnatal depression (Source: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

explanation.summary: Baby blues are transient (days 3-14), self-limiting, and managed with psychoeducation and support; repeat EPDS in 2 weeks screens for evolving postnatal depression.
key_points: Baby blues: 50-80% incidence, peak day 3-5, resolve by day 10-14
Postnatal depression: symptoms beyond 2 weeks, EPDS at least 13 on repeat testing
Postpartum psychosis: typically abrupt onset, days 3-14, urgent admission
Always screen for suicidal and infanticidal thoughts and psychotic features
Involve partner and family in support and monitoring
explanation.pearls: Distinguishing baby blues from early postnatal depression is a temporal call as much as a symptom call; the 2-week repeat is a low-cost, high-value intervention. In context: overtreating baby blues risks unnecessary medication exposure, while undertreating early postnatal depression delays effective care (Source: COPE).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
RCPA thyroid function testing guide

subtopic_detail: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI
stem:
A 32-year-old woman was maintained on sertraline 100 mg orally daily through pregnancy for recurrent major depressive disorder. Her baby was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth and Apgars were 8 and 9. At 6 hours of age the baby, who is otherwise term and vigorous, has developed mild tremor, hypertonia, jitteriness with handling, feeding difficulties, and is grunting intermittently. Axillary temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate 168, respiratory rate 68, and SpO2 96% in air. Bedside glucose is 3.4 mmol/L. There is no maternal history of chorioamnionitis or Group B streptococcus colonisation and there was no prolonged rupture of membranes.

The midwifery team asks whether sertraline should be stopped in the mother and formula introduced.

data_table.Infant at 6 h: Jitteriness, hypertonia, tremor, tachypnoea 68, feeding difficulty; T 36.9, HR 168, SpO2 96% RA, BSL 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit the baby to a neonatal intensive care unit for phenobarbitone treatment of presumed neonatal drug withdrawal and monitor the neonatal abstinence score every 4 hours
options.rationale: SSRI adaptation is self-limited and does not require pharmacotherapy; phenobarbitone is used for opioid neonatal abstinence, not SSRI adaptation. Would never be correct (Source: RCH Neonatal Handbook).
source_refs: RCH Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Full septic workup including blood culture, lumbar puncture, urine culture, and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending cultures at 48 hours
options.rationale: The temporal pattern and typical features (tremor, jitteriness, mild tachypnoea within hours of birth) with no maternal risk factors point to SSRI adaptation, not sepsis; septic workup is not routinely required unless the clinical picture evolves. Would rarely be correct (Source: RCH Neonatal Handbook).
source_refs: RCH Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Stop maternal sertraline immediately, switch the infant to exclusive formula feeding, and monitor maternal mood daily with EPDS by the community midwife
options.rationale: Maternal SSRI cessation in the immediate postpartum period doubles the risk of relapse of depression and does not shorten neonatal adaptation; formula feeding is not indicated for sertraline exposure. Would never be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

options.text: Neonatal observation on the postnatal ward with regular vital signs, feeding support, and glucose monitoring; continue maternal sertraline and encourage breastfeeding
options.rationale: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI exposure is common (up to 30% of exposed infants), typically self-limited over 2-14 days, and managed with observation, feeding support, and glucose monitoring. Maternal sertraline is continued because sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk, breastfeeding provides continuity, and abrupt maternal cessation risks postpartum relapse; formula is not indicated (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP; RCH Neonatal e-Handbook).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
RCH Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Order an urgent echocardiogram to exclude persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, obtain a pre- and post-ductal SpO2, and consider transfer to a tertiary neonatal unit
options.rationale: PPHN is a rare complication (absolute risk about 3 per 1000 exposed) and typically presents with sustained severe hypoxaemia (SpO2 below about 90% or a pre-post ductal difference), not mild self-limited tachypnoea with normal saturations. Would rarely be correct with SpO2 96% (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

explanation.summary: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI exposure is common, self-limited, and managed with observation and feeding support; maternal SSRI is continued, breastfeeding encouraged, and additional interventions reserved for evolving illness.
key_points: Adaptation features: tremor, jitteriness, hypertonia, mild tachypnoea, feeding difficulty
Onset within hours to days; resolves in about 2-14 days
Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk; continue in most cases
PPHN is rare (absolute risk ~3 per 1000 exposed), presents with sustained severe hypoxaemia
Screen the mother for postnatal depression and monitor infant weight and hydration
explanation.pearls: The lay narrative of "SSRI withdrawal" is misleading because the syndrome is thought to reflect neonatal serotonergic effects rather than a physical dependence. In context: continuity of maternal treatment protects both the mother-infant dyad and long-term infant outcomes (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

subtopic_detail: Antenatal SSRI - continue versus stop before delivery
stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation attends her antenatal clinic. She has been on sertraline 100 mg orally daily for recurrent major depressive disorder for 3 years and remained well throughout this pregnancy. She had a severe postpartum relapse after her first pregnancy 4 years ago when she was persuaded to stop her SSRI at 36 weeks. Foetal growth, dopplers, and CTG today are reassuring. Her partner and community midwife are supportive and a joint plan for postpartum care is in place.

Her obstetrician has asked whether her sertraline should be tapered before delivery to "reduce neonatal withdrawal".

data_table.History: Recurrent MDD, on sertraline 100 mg 3 y, well through pregnancy
data_table.Obstetric: 34 weeks; growth, dopplers, CTG reassuring; postpartum relapse in first pregnancy after 36-week SSRI cessation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her sertraline?

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean at 38 weeks to control the timing of SSRI exposure at delivery and to allow the neonate to be admitted directly for observation
options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated for SSRI use and adds surgical and obstetric risks with no benefit; the delivery mode is chosen on obstetric grounds. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 23: Timing of elective caesarean

options.text: Taper sertraline by 25 mg per week to zero by 38 weeks gestation to reduce neonatal adaptation syndrome, and restart sertraline in the immediate postpartum period
options.rationale: Late-pregnancy taper does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation and raises the risk of maternal relapse. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Switch her from sertraline to fluoxetine 20 mg daily, as fluoxetine has a longer half-life and a smoother neonatal course than sertraline in the postpartum period
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has the highest relative infant dose of the SSRIs in breast milk and its long half-life prolongs neonatal exposure; sertraline is preferred. Would never be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Reduce her sertraline dose to 50 mg daily until delivery, then increase again postpartum once the infant is established with feeding and is being monitored by paediatrics
options.rationale: Reducing to a subtherapeutic dose increases the risk of maternal relapse at the highest risk period without meaningful benefit for the neonate; effective dose is maintained. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

options.text: Continue sertraline 100 mg daily through delivery and the postpartum period, plan neonatal observation for adaptation, and maintain postnatal mental health follow-up
options.rationale: Late-pregnancy SSRI cessation does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation syndrome (which is usually mild and self-limited) but substantially increases the risk of maternal relapse in the puerperium (roughly doubling relapse risk), which is worse for the mother-infant dyad than adaptation symptoms. COPE and MotherToBaby Australia advise continuation of a well-tolerated SSRI throughout pregnancy in a woman with recurrent depression, with neonatal observation for adaptation (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Continue an effective SSRI (typically sertraline) through pregnancy and the immediate postpartum period; tapering before delivery does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation syndrome and increases maternal relapse risk.
key_points: Neonatal adaptation syndrome: common (up to 30%), mild, self-limited (2-14 days)
Late-pregnancy taper: no reliable prevention benefit and higher maternal relapse
Postpartum is the highest-risk period for recurrence of mood disorders
Sertraline preferred in breastfeeding (lowest relative infant dose)
Plan neonatal observation, breastfeeding support, and postpartum mental health follow-up
explanation.pearls: In perinatal psychiatry the counter-factual (untreated maternal illness) is the appropriate comparator, not a hypothetical unexposed pregnancy. In context: continuity of effective treatment usually serves both mother and infant better than well-intentioned tapering (Source: COPE).
