subtopic_detail: Prophylaxis after delivery in bipolar I disorder
stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida with bipolar I disorder is seen at 36 weeks in a joint perinatal psychiatry and obstetric clinic. She has been well through pregnancy off medication after psychiatric advice to stop lithium preconception. Her most recent manic episode was 5 years ago and required inpatient care. Her mother had a postpartum psychosis. Foetal growth and welfare are reassuring and vaginal birth is planned.

She strongly wishes to breastfeed. She and her partner are engaged with the perinatal team, and the paediatric team is willing to co-manage.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I; last mania 5 y ago; mother had postpartum psychosis
data_table.Gestation: 36 weeks; foetal welfare reassuring; vaginal birth planned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate postpartum plan to reduce her risk of postpartum psychosis and mania?

options.text: Start sertraline 100 mg orally daily as prophylaxis against postnatal depression, and reassess her mood, sleep, and function fortnightly for the first 3 months postpartum
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I risks precipitating mania; the priority is mood stabiliser prophylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Watchful waiting alone with weekly EPDS monitoring by the community midwife for the first 3 months, and rapid access to acute psychiatry review if any symptoms develop
options.rationale: Watchful waiting misses the window for prophylaxis in the highest-risk period and does not exploit her strong evidence-based option. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Advise her to formula-feed and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily immediately postpartum as the mood stabiliser of choice for postpartum bipolar prophylaxis
options.rationale: Valproate is teratogenic and its use in a woman of reproductive potential requires pregnancy prevention program compliance; it is also not the first-line prophylactic for bipolar I; formula feeding is not necessary for lithium. Would never be correct (Source: AMH; RANZCP).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Introduce prophylactic lithium immediately after delivery with baseline UEC and TSH, lithium level day 5, and paediatric infant monitoring alongside supported breastfeeding
options.rationale: Women with bipolar I disorder have a postpartum psychosis risk of about 20-30% (much higher with a personal or family history), and prophylactic mood stabilisation started at or shortly after delivery substantially reduces recurrence. Lithium is the most evidence-supported prophylactic agent. Contemporary Australian practice (RANZCP, MotherToBaby Australia) accepts lithium in breastfeeding of a well term infant with informed consent, paediatric involvement, and monitoring (Source: RANZCP; MotherToBaby Australia; COPE).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Defer any pharmacological intervention until symptoms of mania or psychosis emerge, then admit for acute treatment with a full mood stabiliser and antipsychotic regimen
options.rationale: Delaying until symptoms emerge is the strategy that failed her mother and is associated with worse outcomes; prophylaxis is the point. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Postpartum prophylactic mood stabilisation (usually lithium) at or shortly after delivery substantially reduces the risk of postpartum psychosis and mania in women with bipolar I disorder; breastfeeding on lithium is acceptable with informed consent and monitoring.
key_points: Recurrence risk in bipolar I postpartum without prophylaxis: about 20-30%; higher with personal or family history of postpartum psychosis
Lithium: strongest evidence for postpartum prophylaxis
Alternatives: olanzapine or quetiapine when lithium is not tolerated or breastfeeding priority
Baseline UEC, TSH before starting lithium; level at day 5 then weekly for 2 weeks
Paediatric monitoring of infant on maternal lithium: serum lithium, UEC, TSH periodically
explanation.pearls: The postpartum period is the highest-risk time for a woman with bipolar I; prevention outperforms rescue. In context: informed shared decision-making about lithium and breastfeeding is a signature perinatal psychiatry conversation (Source: RANZCP).
